## Introduction and overview {#intro}

  -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Module               Foundations of Distributed and Large-Scale Computing Optimization
  Official title       Foundations of Distributed and Large Scale Computing Optimization
  Instructors          E. CHOUZENOUX (master-mva.com, 2026–2027)
  Period               Semester 1 · period 1 (28/09/2026 – 08/01/2027)
  Credits and volume   5 ECTS · 24 h (lectures 24 h) per the Université Paris-Saclay programme table
  Label                [Learning]{.badge .label} · domains on master-mva.com: Theory
  Language             Not displayed (the master-mva.com course description is written in English)
  Assessment           Two lab reports and an exam (master-mva.com: “2 labs report + exam”; no weights displayed); Université Paris-Saclay: “Evaluation Continue non Intégrale” (partial continuous assessment)
  Prerequisites        Not displayed
  Note on sources      master-mva.com announces 7 sessions of 3 h plus a 2 h exam; the Université Paris-Saclay table gives 24 h of lectures, the volume used in the session plan
  -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Audience**: a student with a good M1 in applied mathematics, computer science or signal processing who can minimize a smooth convex function by gradient descent and now faces problems with millions of unknowns, non-smooth regularizers, or data spread over several machines.

**Empirical first**: on a denoising problem with 2000 unknowns and an edge-preserving penalty, plain gradient descent still has an objective error of 25.6 after 50 iterations. A Majorization–Minimization method of about the same cost per iteration is at $2.8 \times 10^{-7}$ ([ch. 5](#ch5)). On a ring of 10 machines holding different data, decentralized gradient descent stalls at distance 0.42 from the solution forever, while gradient tracking reaches machine precision ([ch. 8](#ch8)).

This course explains both observations. It builds the convex-analytic toolbox (proximity operators, monotone operators, majorants) behind the algorithms that solve very large problems. It then shows how the same algorithms split across the cores of one machine or across a network of machines.

The course shares tools with [Convex Optimization and Applications in Machine Learning](../s1-convex-optimization/index.html), taught in the same semester, and prepares the imaging and large-model courses of semester 2, such as [Deep Learning for Image Restoration and Synthesis](../s2-dl-image-restoration-synthesis/index.html) and [Training and Deploying Large-Scale Models](../s2-training-deploying-large-models/index.html).

### What you will be able to do

-   Compute the proximity operator of the usual regularizers and constraints, and combine them with the rules of proximal calculus.
-   Prove the convergence rates of gradient descent, forward–backward and FISTA from the descent lemma.
-   Choose between forward–backward, Douglas–Rachford, ADMM and primal–dual methods from the structure of a problem.
-   Build a tangent majorant for a given cost (Lipschitz, half-quadratic, Jensen) and derive the Majorization–Minimization algorithm it defines.
-   Implement the subspace Majorization–Minimization method 3MG and explain why it scales to large images.
-   Analyze stochastic gradient, variance-reduced and randomized coordinate methods on finite sums.
-   Reformulate a sum of functions in a product space and run the parallel proximal algorithm PPXA.
-   Predict the speedup of a parallel method with Amdahl's law, the cost of an all-reduce and the damping of parallel coordinate steps.
-   Design a distributed method (consensus ADMM, decentralized gradient, gradient tracking) for data held by several agents, and explain the bias of naive schemes.
-   Implement these methods in NumPy and PyTorch and check them against a reference solution.

### Official objectives and syllabus (2026–2027)

The course description on master-mva.com states as objective to introduce the theoretical background that makes it possible to develop efficient algorithms for the large-scale problems the course addresses, taking advantage of modern multicore or distributed computing architectures.

The description adds that the course is mainly focused on nonlinear optimization tools for convex problems. It presents proximal tools, splitting techniques and Majorization–Minimization strategies, which the description calls very popular for processing massive data sets, and it illustrates these methods on various application examples.

The listed instructor is Emilie Chouzenoux (CentraleSupélec & INRIA Saclay). The organisation announced is 7 sessions of 3 h plus a 2 h exam, and the assessment is two lab reports plus an exam. ### Where this course fits in the programme

Official prerequisites: not displayed. In practice the course uses M1 linear algebra (eigenvalues, symmetric matrices), differential calculus and the basics of convex functions; ch. 0 reviews what is needed. Chapter 6 also uses expectations and variances.

-   **Refreshers** — [Linear Algebra, Analysis and Optimization](../s0-refresher-linear-algebra-optimization/index.html) for ch. 0, [Probability and Statistics](../s0-refresher-probability-statistics/index.html) for the stochastic methods of ch. 6, and [Scientific Python, NumPy and PyTorch](../s0-refresher-python-scientific-computing/index.html) for the code.
-   **Related courses of semester 1** — [Convex Optimization and Applications in Machine Learning](../s1-convex-optimization/index.html) (duality and interior-point methods, complementary to the first-order methods here), [Computational Statistics](../s1-computational-statistics/index.html) (EM and stochastic approximation, met as MM and SGD), [Introduction to Probabilistic Graphical Models](../s1-probabilistic-graphical-models/index.html) (EM), [Deep Learning](../s1-deep-learning/index.html) (stochastic training), [Optimal Transport](../s1-optimal-transport-ml/index.html) (entropic solvers as alternating projections) and [Image Denoising](../s1-image-denoising/index.html) (variational denoisers).
-   **Semester 2 courses that build on it** — [Deep Learning for Image Restoration and Synthesis](../s2-dl-image-restoration-synthesis/index.html) (variational and hybrid methods for inverse problems), [Inverse Problems and Imaging](../s2-inverse-problems-imaging/index.html) (regularized least squares for ill-posed problems), [Training and Deploying Large-Scale Models](../s2-training-deploying-large-models/index.html) (data parallelism and all-reduce), [Algorithms for Network Optimization and Management](../s2-network-optimization/index.html) (optimization problems of communication networks), [Graphs in Machine Learning](../s2-graphs-in-ml/index.html) (graph Laplacians, the matrices of gossip), [Sequential Learning](../s2-sequential-learning/index.html) (online convex optimization) and [Kernel Methods](../s2-kernel-methods/index.html) (large-scale kernel solvers).

### Course outline

-   **0. Review: convex analysis and gradient descent** — subdifferentials, smoothness and strong convexity, the rates of gradient descent, conjugates and Fenchel duality.
-   **1. Large-scale optimization** — the composite model, what second-order methods cost, the lower bound of first-order methods, acceleration, estimating Lipschitz constants and preconditioning.
-   **2. Proximity operators** — definition, a catalogue, firm nonexpansiveness, Moreau decomposition and envelope, proximal calculus.
-   **3. Proximal gradient algorithms** — forward–backward, its $O(1/k)$ rate, FISTA and its $O(1/k^2)$ rate, variable metrics.
-   **4. Splitting algorithms** — averaged operators, Douglas–Rachford, ADMM, Chambolle–Pock and Condat–Vũ.
-   **5. Majorization–Minimization** — tangent majorants, half-quadratic and EM, convergence, the subspace method 3MG.
-   **6. Stochastic and block-coordinate methods** — stochastic gradient, mini-batches, SVRG and SAGA, randomized coordinate descent.
-   **7. Parallel optimization** — speedup and communication models, PPXA in a product space, parallel coordinate descent, data parallelism and asynchrony.
-   **8. Distributed optimization strategies** — consensus ADMM, gossip, decentralized gradient, gradient tracking, federated averaging.
-   **9. Research directions and open problems** — a self-study tour of current work.

### How to study this module

-   Read ch. 0 before session 1 if subdifferentials or conjugate functions feel distant: every later proof uses them.
-   Follow one thread through the course: almost every algorithm is a fixed-point iteration of an averaged operator (ch. 4), and almost every proof is the descent lemma of ch. 0 plus one inequality.
-   After each session, do the exercises listed in its row, then run the code of the chapter and change one parameter (step size, number of workers, graph) to see the effect predicted by the theory.
-   The code uses NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn, NetworkX and PyTorch (CPU) on synthetic data; every block runs in a few seconds on a laptop.
-   The solo projects of the last section are sized like the two official lab reports; start the first one after session 3.

## 0. Review: convex analysis and gradient descent {#ch0}

Every algorithm of the course minimizes a convex function that may be non-smooth or take the value $+\infty$. This chapter collects the M1-level facts the proofs rely on: subgradients, the descent lemma, the rates of gradient descent and Fenchel duality.

The [Linear Algebra, Analysis and Optimization refresher](../s0-refresher-linear-algebra-optimization/index.html) covers the same ground at a slower pace. Throughout, the space is $\mathbb{R}^N$ with the Euclidean inner product $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$; all results hold in Hilbert spaces (Bauschke and Combettes, 2011).

### Convex functions and subdifferentials

::: def
[Definition 0.1 — The class Γ₀]{.tag} A function $f : \mathbb{R}^N \to (-\infty, +\infty]$ is **proper** if its domain $\mathrm{dom} f = \{x : f(x) < +\infty\}$ is non-empty, **convex** if its epigraph is convex, and **lower semicontinuous** if its epigraph is closed.

$\Gamma_0(\mathbb{R}^N)$ denotes the proper, convex, lower semicontinuous functions. Examples: every norm; every convex quadratic; the **indicator** of a non-empty closed convex set $C$,
$$
\iota_C(x) = 0 \ \text{ if } x \in C, \qquad \iota_C(x) = +\infty \ \text{ otherwise}.
$$
:::

Indicators turn constraints into terms of the objective: minimizing $f$ over $C$ is minimizing $f + \iota_C$ over the whole space.

::: def
[Definition 0.2 — Subdifferential]{.tag} The subdifferential of $f \in \Gamma_0(\mathbb{R}^N)$ at $x$ is the set of slopes of affine minorants that touch $f$ at $x$:
$$
\partial f(x) = \{ u \in \mathbb{R}^N : f(y) \geq f(x) + \langle u, y - x \rangle \ \text{ for all } y \}.
$$
If $f$ is differentiable at $x$, then $\partial f(x) = \{\nabla f(x)\}$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.3 — Fermat's rule and the sum rule]{.tag}

1.  A point $x^\star$ minimizes $f$ if and only if $0 \in \partial f(x^\star)$.
2.  If $f, g \in \Gamma_0(\mathbb{R}^N)$ and one of them is finite and continuous everywhere, then $\partial (f + g) = \partial f + \partial g$.

::: proof
Item 1 is the definition read with $u = 0$: the inequality $f(y) \geq f(x^\star)$ for all $y$. Item 2 is the Moreau–Rockafellar theorem; its proof uses a separating hyperplane (Bauschke and Combettes, 2011, ch. 16). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 0.4 — Two subdifferentials and the optimality of the lasso]{.tag}

-   For the absolute value, $\partial |\cdot|(x) = \{\mathrm{sign}(x)\}$ if $x \neq 0$, and $\partial |\cdot|(0) = [-1, 1]$.
-   For an indicator, $\partial \iota_C(x)$ is the normal cone: the vectors $u$ with $\langle u, y - x \rangle \leq 0$ for every $y \in C$.

For the lasso $F(x) = \frac12 \|Ax - b\|^2 + \lambda \|x\|_1$, the sum rule and Fermat's rule give the optimality conditions, coordinate by coordinate, with $a_j$ the $j$-th column of $A$:
$$
a_j^\top (b - A x^\star) = \lambda\, \mathrm{sign}(x^\star_j) \ \text{ if } x^\star_j \neq 0, \qquad |a_j^\top (b - A x^\star)| \leq \lambda \ \text{ if } x^\star_j = 0.
$$
In particular $x^\star = 0$ is optimal exactly when $\|A^\top b\|_\infty \leq \lambda$.
:::

### Smoothness, strong convexity and gradient descent

::: def
[Definition 0.5 — Smoothness and strong convexity]{.tag} A differentiable $f$ is **$L$-smooth** if its gradient is $L$-Lipschitz:
$$
\|\nabla f(x) - \nabla f(y)\| \leq L \|x - y\| .
$$
It is **$\mu$-strongly convex** ($\mu > 0$) if $f - \frac{\mu}{2}\|\cdot\|^2$ is convex. The ratio $\kappa = L / \mu$ is the **condition number**.

For a quadratic $\frac12 x^\top Q x - c^\top x$ with $Q$ symmetric positive definite, $L$ and $\mu$ are the largest and smallest eigenvalues of $Q$.
:::

:::: prop
[Lemma 0.6 — Descent lemma]{.tag} If $f$ is $L$-smooth, then for all $x, y$:
$$
f(y) \leq f(x) + \langle \nabla f(x), y - x \rangle + \frac{L}{2} \|y - x\|^2 .
$$

::: proof
Write $f(y) - f(x) - \langle \nabla f(x), y - x\rangle$ as the integral over $t \in [0, 1]$ of $\langle \nabla f(x + t(y - x)) - \nabla f(x), y - x \rangle$. By Cauchy–Schwarz and the Lipschitz bound, the integrand is at most $L t \|y - x\|^2$, whose integral is $\frac{L}{2}\|y - x\|^2$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The descent lemma says that a smooth function lies below a parabola tangent at any point. Minimizing that parabola is a gradient step: it is the first Majorization–Minimization algorithm of the course ([ch. 5](#ch5)).

:::: thm
[Theorem 0.7 — Rates of gradient descent]{.tag} Let $f$ be convex and $L$-smooth with a minimizer $x^\star$, and let $x_{k+1} = x_k - \frac{1}{L} \nabla f(x_k)$. Then $f(x_k)$ is non-increasing and
$$
f(x_k) - f(x^\star) \leq \frac{L\, \|x_0 - x^\star\|^2}{2k} .
$$
If moreover $f$ is $\mu$-strongly convex, the iterates converge linearly:
$$
\|x_k - x^\star\|^2 \leq \Big(1 - \frac{\mu}{L}\Big)^k \|x_0 - x^\star\|^2 .
$$

::: proof
Write $g = \nabla f(x)$ and $x^+ = x - g / L$.

1.  The descent lemma at $y = x^+$ gives $f(x^+) \leq f(x) - \frac{1}{2L}\|g\|^2$: the values decrease.
2.  Convexity gives $f(x) \leq f(x^\star) + \langle g, x - x^\star \rangle$.
3.  Adding the two and completing the square:
    $$
    f(x^+) - f(x^\star) \leq \langle g, x - x^\star \rangle - \frac{\|g\|^2}{2L} = \frac{L}{2}\big( \|x - x^\star\|^2 - \|x^+ - x^\star\|^2 \big).
    $$
4.  Summing over the first $k$ steps telescopes the right-hand side, bounded by $\frac{L}{2}\|x_0 - x^\star\|^2$. The left-hand terms decrease, so the last one is at most their mean.

With strong convexity, step 2 improves by $-\frac{\mu}{2}\|x - x^\star\|^2$. Since the left-hand side of step 3 is non-negative, $\|x^+ - x^\star\|^2 \leq (1 - \mu / L)\|x - x^\star\|^2$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

To reach a relative accuracy $\varepsilon$ on $\|x_k - x^\star\|^2$, the linear rate needs about $\kappa \ln(1/\varepsilon)$ iterations. Chapter 1 shows that this dependence on $\kappa$ is not optimal.

### Conjugates and duality

::: def
[Definition 0.8 — Fenchel conjugate]{.tag} The conjugate of $f$ is
$$
f^*(u) = \sup_{x \in \mathbb{R}^N} \; \langle u, x \rangle - f(x) .
$$
For $f \in \Gamma_0(\mathbb{R}^N)$: $f^* \in \Gamma_0(\mathbb{R}^N)$ and $f^{**} = f$ (Fenchel–Moreau).

The **Fenchel–Young inequality** $f(x) + f^*(u) \geq \langle u, x \rangle$ holds for all $x, u$. Equality holds if and only if $u \in \partial f(x)$, equivalently $x \in \partial f^*(u)$.
:::

::: ex
[Example 0.9 — Four conjugates used later]{.tag}

-   $\frac12 \|\cdot\|^2$ is its own conjugate.
-   The conjugate of a norm is the indicator of the unit ball of the dual norm. For instance, the conjugate of $\lambda \|\cdot\|_1$ is the indicator of the box $\{u : \|u\|_\infty \leq \lambda\}$.
-   The conjugate of $\iota_C$ is the support function $\sigma_C(u) = \sup_{x \in C} \langle u, x \rangle$.
-   If $g(x) = \frac12 \|x - y\|^2$, then $g^*(u) = \frac12 \|u\|^2 + \langle u, y \rangle$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.10 — Fenchel–Rockafellar duality]{.tag} Let $f \in \Gamma_0(\mathbb{R}^N)$, $h \in \Gamma_0(\mathbb{R}^M)$ and $K \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times N}$. Consider the primal and dual problems
$$
p^\star = \inf_x \; f(x) + h(Kx), \qquad d^\star = \sup_u \; -f^*(-K^\top u) - h^*(u) .
$$

1.  **Weak duality**: $d^\star \leq p^\star$.
2.  **Strong duality**: if $0$ is an interior point of $\mathrm{dom}\, h - K \mathrm{dom} f$, then $p^\star = d^\star$ and the dual supremum is attained.
3.  **Optimality**: $(x^\star, u^\star)$ is a primal–dual solution if and only if
    $$
    -K^\top u^\star \in \partial f(x^\star) \qquad \text{and} \qquad u^\star \in \partial h(K x^\star) .
    $$

::: proof
Weak duality: Fenchel–Young gives $f(x) + f^*(-K^\top u) \geq -\langle u, Kx \rangle$ and $h(Kx) + h^*(u) \geq \langle u, Kx \rangle$; add them. Item 3 is the equality case of both inequalities. Item 2 needs a separation argument (Bauschke and Combettes, 2011, ch. 15). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The dual variable $u$ lives in the space of $Kx$. Primal–dual algorithms ([ch. 4](#ch4)) update $x$ and $u$ together and only ever multiply by $K$ and $K^\top$.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 0

-   Constraints become indicator functions; Fermat's rule $0 \in \partial f(x^\star)$ characterizes minimizers, and the sum rule splits the subdifferential of a sum.
-   The descent lemma bounds an $L$-smooth function by a tangent parabola; gradient descent with step $1/L$ minimizes that parabola.
-   Gradient descent reaches $O(1/k)$ on convex smooth functions and a linear rate $(1 - 1/\kappa)^k$ under strong convexity.
-   Conjugates turn norms into indicators of dual balls, and Fenchel–Rockafellar duality pairs $f + h \circ K$ with a dual problem in the space of $Kx$.
:::

## 1. Large-scale optimization: models, costs and accelerated gradients {#ch1}

What makes an optimization problem "large", and which algorithms survive at that scale? This chapter fixes the model problem of the course, shows why second-order methods are out of reach, and establishes what first-order methods can and cannot achieve.

### The model problem

Most problems of the course have the composite form
$$
\min_{x \in \mathbb{R}^N} \; F(x) = \sum_{j=1}^{J} f_j(L_j x),
$$
with each $f_j \in \Gamma_0$ simple in some sense (smooth, or with an explicit proximity operator) and each $L_j$ a linear operator that can be applied quickly.

::: ex
[Example 1.1 — Four large problems]{.tag}

1.  **Image restoration.** An image $\bar x$ of $N = 10^6$ pixels is observed as $y = H \bar x + w$, with a blur $H$ and noise $w$. The estimate minimizes a data term plus a regularization, such as total variation with $D$ the discrete gradient:
    $$
    \tfrac12 \|Hx - y\|^2 + \lambda \|D x\|_{1} .
    $$
2.  **Sparse regression (lasso).** In genomics, $N$ can reach $10^5$ to $10^6$ features for a few thousand samples, and the cost is $\frac12 \|Ax - b\|^2 + \lambda \|x\|_1$.
3.  **Regularized logistic regression.** For click prediction, the number $n$ of samples $(a_i, b_i)$ can exceed $10^9$:
    $$
    \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \log\big(1 + e^{-b_i a_i^\top x}\big) + \frac{\mu}{2}\|x\|^2 .
    $$
4.  **Training a neural network.** The same finite-sum structure, with a non-convex loss and up to $10^{11}$ parameters.
:::

"Large" means that $N$, $n$ or both are too large for any method whose cost per iteration grows faster than linearly with the size of the data.

::: ex
[Example 1.2 — What a Newton step would cost]{.tag} Take a $1000 \times 1000$ image, so $N = 10^6$.

-   A dense Hessian has $N^2 = 10^{12}$ entries, that is 8 TB in double precision.
-   A Cholesky factorization costs about $N^3 / 3 \approx 3.3 \times 10^{17}$ flops: about four days at $10^{12}$ flop/s.
-   A product by a convolution $H$ costs $O(N \log N)$ with the FFT, about $2 \times 10^7$ flops: a few tens of microseconds at the same speed.

The algorithms of this course use only products by $L_j$ and $L_j^\top$, gradients and simple proximity operators, so that one iteration costs about as much as reading the data.
:::

### What first-order methods can achieve

::: def
[Definition 1.3 — First-order method]{.tag} A first-order method on a differentiable $f$ generates iterates in the span of the gradients seen so far:
$$
x_k \in x_0 + \mathrm{span}\{\nabla f(x_0), \dots, \nabla f(x_{k-1})\} .
$$
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 1.4 — Lower bound for smooth convex minimization]{.tag} For every $k$ with $1 \leq k \leq (N - 1)/2$ and every $x_0$, there is a convex $L$-smooth function on $\mathbb{R}^N$ such that every first-order method satisfies
$$
f(x_k) - f(x^\star) \geq \frac{3 L\, \|x_0 - x^\star\|^2}{32\, (k + 1)^2} .
$$

::: proof
*Sketch* (Nesterov, 2004, §2.1.2). The worst function is a quadratic whose matrix is the Laplacian of a path graph, $\frac{L}{4}$ times the tridiagonal matrix with $2$ on the diagonal and $-1$ beside it, plus a linear term on the first coordinate.

Starting from $0$, each gradient makes at most one new coordinate non-zero: information travels one coordinate per iteration. After $k$ steps the iterate lives in the first $k$ coordinates, while the minimizer has all coordinates non-zero. A direct computation of the best value on that subspace gives the bound. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Gradient descent reaches $O(1/k)$ (Theorem 0.7), while the bound allows $O(1/k^2)$. Nesterov (1983) closed the gap with a momentum term.

::: thm
[Algorithm 1.5 — Nesterov's accelerated gradient]{.tag} Set $y_1 = x_0$ and $t_1 = 1$. For $k \geq 1$:
$$
x_k = y_k - \tfrac{1}{L} \nabla f(y_k), \qquad t_{k+1} = \frac{1 + \sqrt{1 + 4 t_k^2}}{2}, \qquad y_{k+1} = x_k + \frac{t_k - 1}{t_{k+1}}\,(x_k - x_{k-1}) .
$$
The gradient is taken at the extrapolated point $y_k$, not at $x_k$.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 1.6 — Rates of the accelerated gradient]{.tag} If $f$ is convex and $L$-smooth, Algorithm 1.5 satisfies
$$
f(x_k) - f(x^\star) \leq \frac{2 L\, \|x_0 - x^\star\|^2}{(k + 1)^2},
$$
which matches Theorem 1.4 up to a constant. If $f$ is $\mu$-strongly convex, a constant momentum $(\sqrt{\kappa} - 1)/(\sqrt{\kappa} + 1)$ gives a linear rate of order $(1 - 1/\sqrt{\kappa})^k$ (Nesterov, 2004, §2.2).

::: proof
The first bound is the case $g = 0$ of Theorem 3.6, proved in [ch. 3](#ch3) for the more general proximal setting. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The gain is large on ill-conditioned problems. With $\kappa = 10^4$ and $\varepsilon = 10^{-6}$, the two iteration counts are
$$
\kappa \ln(1/\varepsilon) \approx 1.4 \times 10^5 \ \text{ (gradient descent)}, \qquad \sqrt{\kappa} \ln(1/\varepsilon) \approx 1.4 \times 10^3 \ \text{ (accelerated)}.
$$

### Estimating the Lipschitz constant

Every method above needs $L$, and a step larger than $2/L$ can diverge. For $f(x) = \frac12 \|Ax - b\|^2$, the constant is $L = \|A\|^2$, the largest eigenvalue of $A^\top A$, which is too costly to compute exactly at scale.

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.7 — Power iteration]{.tag} Let $M = A^\top A$ have eigenvalues $\lambda_1 > \lambda_2 \geq \dots \geq 0$. For a random start $v_0$, the iteration $v_{k+1} = M v_k / \|M v_k\|$ satisfies
$$
v_k^\top M v_k \longrightarrow \lambda_1 = \|A\|^2,
$$
with an error of order $(\lambda_2 / \lambda_1)^{2k}$. Each step costs one product by $A$ and one by $A^\top$.

::: proof
Expand $v_0 = \sum_i c_i u_i$ in an orthonormal eigenbasis; $c_1 \neq 0$ with probability one. Then $M^k v_0 = \sum_i c_i \lambda_i^k u_i$ aligns with $u_1$ at the rate $(\lambda_2/\lambda_1)^k$. The Rayleigh quotient is quadratic in the error on the direction, which squares the rate. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### Preconditioning

Ill-conditioning slows every first-order method. A preconditioner changes the geometry in which the gradient step is taken.

::: def
[Definition 1.8 — Preconditioned gradient step]{.tag} For a symmetric positive definite $P$, write $\|x\|_P^2 = x^\top P x$. The preconditioned step is
$$
x^+ = x - P^{-1} \nabla f(x) .
$$
Suppose that, for all $x, y$,
$$
f(y) \leq f(x) + \langle \nabla f(x), y - x\rangle + \tfrac12 \|y - x\|_P^2,
$$
for instance when $\nabla^2 f \preceq P$. Then the step minimizes this upper bound and decreases $f$ by at least $\frac12 \nabla f(x)^\top P^{-1} \nabla f(x)$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.9 — A diagonal majorant]{.tag} For a symmetric matrix $M$, let $P = \mathrm{diag}(p)$ with $p_i = \sum_j |M_{ij}|$. Then $M \preceq P$.

::: proof
For every $x$, using $|x_i x_j| \leq \frac12 (x_i^2 + x_j^2)$ and the symmetry of $M$:
$$
x^\top M x \leq \sum_{i,j} |M_{ij}|\, |x_i|\, |x_j| \leq \sum_{i} \Big(\sum_j |M_{ij}|\Big) x_i^2 = x^\top P x .
$$
[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

A diagonal preconditioner costs nothing to invert, and its step updates all coordinates independently. This is the first example of a *separable* majorant, which makes an algorithm parallel ([ch. 5](#ch5) and [ch. 7](#ch7)).

The code below estimates $L$ by power iteration on an ill-conditioned least-squares problem (singular values of the design spread over two decades), then compares gradient descent and Algorithm 1.5.

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n, d = 300, 200
A = rng.standard_normal((n, d)) @ np.diag(np.logspace(0, -2, d))  # ill-conditioned
x_true = rng.standard_normal(d)
b = A @ x_true + 0.01 * rng.standard_normal(n)

# Lipschitz constant of grad f, f(x) = 0.5 ||Ax - b||^2, by power iteration
v = rng.standard_normal(d)
for _ in range(100):
    v = A.T @ (A @ v)
    v /= np.linalg.norm(v)
L = v @ (A.T @ (A @ v))
print(f"power iteration L = {L:.4f}, exact ||A||^2 = {np.linalg.norm(A, 2)**2:.4f}")

f = lambda x: 0.5 * np.sum((A @ x - b) ** 2)
f_star = f(np.linalg.lstsq(A, b, rcond=None)[0])
grad = lambda x: A.T @ (A @ x - b)

x = np.zeros(d)                           # gradient descent, step 1/L
y, z, t = np.zeros(d), np.zeros(d), 1.0   # Nesterov (FISTA with g = 0)
for k in range(1, 501):
    x = x - grad(x) / L
    z_new = y - grad(y) / L
    t_new = (1 + np.sqrt(1 + 4 * t * t)) / 2
    y = z_new + (t - 1) / t_new * (z_new - z)
    z, t = z_new, t_new
    if k in (10, 100, 500):
        print(f"k={k:4d}  GD gap {f(x) - f_star:.3e}   Nesterov gap {f(z) - f_star:.3e}")
```

Power iteration recovers $L = 348.1558$ to all printed digits. After 500 iterations the objective gaps are
$$
\text{gradient descent: } 2.81, \qquad \text{accelerated: } 7.6 \times 10^{-3} .
$$
At $k = 100$ the gaps are already 15.3 and 0.86.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 1

-   Large-scale problems are sums of simple functions composed with fast linear operators; one iteration should cost about one pass over the data.
-   Newton steps are out of reach at $N = 10^6$ (terabytes, days); first-order methods use only gradients, products by $L_j$, $L_j^\top$ and simple proximity operators.
-   No first-order method beats $O(1/k^2)$ on smooth convex functions; Nesterov's momentum attains it, and replaces $\kappa$ by $\sqrt{\kappa}$ in the linear rate.
-   Power iteration estimates $L$ cheaply; diagonal majorants give free, separable preconditioners.
:::

## 2. Proximity operators {#ch2}

Gradient steps need differentiability, and the $\ell_1$ norm, total variation or a constraint are not differentiable. The proximity operator replaces the gradient step on such a term by a small, often explicit, minimization problem.

### Definition and catalogue

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — Proximity operator]{.tag} For $f \in \Gamma_0(\mathbb{R}^N)$ and $\gamma > 0$, the proximity operator of $\gamma f$ at $v$ is
$$
\mathrm{prox}_{\gamma f}(v) = \operatorname*{argmin}_{x \in \mathbb{R}^N} \; f(x) + \frac{1}{2\gamma} \|x - v\|^2 .
$$
It is a compromise between minimizing $f$ and staying close to $v$; $\gamma$ sets the balance.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.2 — Existence, uniqueness, characterization]{.tag} The minimizer in Definition 2.1 exists and is unique, and
$$
p = \mathrm{prox}_{\gamma f}(v) \iff v - p \in \gamma\, \partial f(p) .
$$

::: proof
The objective is in $\Gamma_0$ and $\frac{1}{\gamma}$-strongly convex, hence coercive: a minimizer exists, and strict convexity makes it unique. The quadratic term is finite and differentiable everywhere, so the sum rule and Fermat's rule (Proposition 0.3) give $0 \in \partial f(p) + (p - v)/\gamma$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The inclusion reads $p = (I + \gamma \partial f)^{-1}(v)$: the prox is an **implicit** (backward) gradient step, where the subgradient is taken at the arrival point.

::: ex
[Example 2.3 — A catalogue of proximity operators]{.tag}

1.  **Indicator.** $\mathrm{prox}_{\gamma \iota_C} = P_C$, the projection onto $C$, for every $\gamma$. For a box, it clips each coordinate.
2.  **$\ell_1$ norm.** The prox of $\gamma \|\cdot\|_1$ is **soft thresholding**, coordinate by coordinate:
    $$
    \big(\mathrm{prox}_{\gamma \|\cdot\|_1}(v)\big)_i = \mathrm{sign}(v_i)\, \max(|v_i| - \gamma, 0) .
    $$
    In one dimension, Proposition 2.2 gives $p = v - \gamma$ if $v > \gamma$, $p = v + \gamma$ if $v < -\gamma$, and $p = 0$ exactly when $|v| \leq \gamma$.
3.  **Least squares.** For $f(x) = \frac12 \|Ax - b\|^2$, setting the gradient to zero gives a linear system:
    $$
    \mathrm{prox}_{\gamma f}(v) = (I + \gamma A^\top A)^{-1} (v + \gamma A^\top b) .
    $$
4.  **Euclidean norm** (group sparsity). The prox of $\gamma \|\cdot\|_2$ shrinks the whole vector:
    $$
    \mathrm{prox}_{\gamma \|\cdot\|_2}(v) = \max\Big(1 - \frac{\gamma}{\|v\|_2},\, 0\Big)\, v .
    $$
5.  **Separable sums.** If $f(x) = \sum_i f_i(x_i)$ over blocks $x_i$, the prox acts block by block, and the blocks can be processed in parallel.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.4 — Fixed points and the proximal point algorithm]{.tag} For every $\gamma > 0$,
$$
x^\star \in \operatorname{argmin} f \iff x^\star = \mathrm{prox}_{\gamma f}(x^\star) .
$$

::: proof
By Proposition 2.2, $x^\star = \mathrm{prox}_{\gamma f}(x^\star)$ if and only if $0 \in \gamma\, \partial f(x^\star)$, which is Fermat's rule. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The **proximal point algorithm** $x_{k+1} = \mathrm{prox}_{\gamma f}(x_k)$ converges to a minimizer of $f$ whenever one exists (Rockafellar, 1976). It is rarely practical on its own, since each step is as hard as the original problem, but it is the template of every algorithm of chapters 3 and 4.

### Firm nonexpansiveness and Moreau's identities

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.5 — Firm nonexpansiveness]{.tag} For all $u, w$, with $p = \mathrm{prox}_{\gamma f}(u)$ and $q = \mathrm{prox}_{\gamma f}(w)$:
$$
\|p - q\|^2 \leq \langle p - q,\, u - w \rangle .
$$
In particular, $\|p - q\| \leq \|u - w\|$: the prox is nonexpansive.

::: proof
First, $\partial f$ is **monotone**: if $a \in \partial f(p)$ and $c \in \partial f(q)$, adding the two subgradient inequalities between $p$ and $q$ gives $\langle a - c, p - q \rangle \geq 0$.

By Proposition 2.2, $(u - p)/\gamma \in \partial f(p)$ and $(w - q)/\gamma \in \partial f(q)$. Monotonicity gives $\langle (u - w) - (p - q),\, p - q \rangle \geq 0$, which is the claim. Cauchy–Schwarz then gives nonexpansiveness. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.6 — Moreau decomposition]{.tag} For $f \in \Gamma_0(\mathbb{R}^N)$, $\gamma > 0$ and every $v$:
$$
v = \mathrm{prox}_{\gamma f}(v) + \gamma\, \mathrm{prox}_{\gamma^{-1} f^*}(v / \gamma) .
$$

::: proof
Let $p = \mathrm{prox}_{\gamma f}(v)$ and $u = (v - p)/\gamma$.

1.  By Proposition 2.2, $u \in \partial f(p)$.
2.  By the equality case of Fenchel–Young (Definition 0.8), $p \in \partial f^*(u)$.
3.  Hence $v/\gamma - u = p/\gamma \in \partial (\gamma^{-1} f^*)(u)$, which by Proposition 2.2 (with parameter 1) means $u = \mathrm{prox}_{\gamma^{-1} f^*}(v/\gamma)$.

Then $v = p + \gamma u$ is the claim. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

When $f$ is a norm, $f^*$ is the indicator of the dual unit ball (Example 0.9), and scaling an indicator changes nothing. The prox of a norm is therefore the identity minus a projection: soft thresholding is $v - P_{[-\gamma, \gamma]^N}(v)$. This identity also gives the prox of a conjugate, which the primal–dual methods of [ch. 4](#ch4) need.

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.7 — Moreau envelope]{.tag} The Moreau envelope of $f \in \Gamma_0(\mathbb{R}^N)$ is
$$
{}^{\gamma} f(v) = \min_x \; f(x) + \frac{1}{2\gamma}\|x - v\|^2 .
$$
It is convex, finite everywhere, has the same minimizers as $f$, and is differentiable with a $\frac{1}{\gamma}$-Lipschitz gradient:
$$
\nabla\, {}^{\gamma} f(v) = \frac{v - \mathrm{prox}_{\gamma f}(v)}{\gamma} .
$$

::: proof
*Sketch.* The gradient formula is proved in Bauschke and Combettes (2011, ch. 12). By Theorem 2.6, the gradient equals $\mathrm{prox}_{\gamma^{-1} f^*}(v/\gamma)$, which is nonexpansive in $v/\gamma$, hence $\frac1\gamma$-Lipschitz in $v$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 2.8 — The Huber function]{.tag} The Moreau envelope of $|\cdot|$ is the Huber function:
$$
{}^{\gamma} |\cdot|(v) = \frac{v^2}{2\gamma} \ \text{ if } |v| \leq \gamma, \qquad {}^{\gamma} |\cdot|(v) = |v| - \frac{\gamma}{2} \ \text{ otherwise.}
$$
For $|v| > \gamma$, the prox is $v - \gamma\, \mathrm{sign}(v)$, and the value is $|v| - \gamma + \gamma/2$. Smoothing a non-smooth term by its envelope lets gradient methods handle it, at the price of a bias of size $\gamma/2$.
:::

### Proximal calculus

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.9 — Three rules]{.tag}

1.  **Translation.** If $g(x) = f(x - a)$, then
    $$
    \mathrm{prox}_{\gamma g}(v) = a + \mathrm{prox}_{\gamma f}(v - a) .
    $$
2.  **Quadratic perturbation.** If $g(x) = f(x) + \frac{\alpha}{2}\|x\|^2$ with $\alpha \geq 0$, then
    $$
    \mathrm{prox}_{\gamma g}(v) = \mathrm{prox}_{\frac{\gamma}{1 + \alpha\gamma} f}\Big(\frac{v}{1 + \alpha \gamma}\Big) .
    $$
3.  **Semi-orthogonal composition.** If $g = f \circ L$ with $L L^\top = \nu I$ for some $\nu > 0$ (an orthogonal transform, or a tight frame), then
    $$
    \mathrm{prox}_{\gamma g}(v) = v + \nu^{-1} L^\top \big( \mathrm{prox}_{\gamma \nu f}(L v) - L v \big) .
    $$

::: proof
Items 1 and 2 follow by a change of variable and by completing the square in Definition 2.1. Item 3 is proved in Bauschke and Combettes (2011, ch. 24): write $x = L^\top z / \nu + x_\perp$ with $L x_\perp = 0$, and minimize separately over the two components. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Rule 3 covers $\ell_1$ regularization in an orthonormal wavelet or cosine basis. It does not cover total variation, because the discrete gradient $D$ is not semi-orthogonal. In general, the prox of a sum is not the composition of the proxes: that is why splitting algorithms exist ([ch. 4](#ch4)).

The code checks soft thresholding, the Moreau decomposition for the $\ell_1$ norm and firm nonexpansiveness on random pairs.

```python
import numpy as np

def prox_l1(v, gamma):
    """prox of gamma * ||.||_1: soft thresholding"""
    return np.sign(v) * np.maximum(np.abs(v) - gamma, 0.0) + 0.0

def proj_linf(v, r):
    """projection onto the l-infinity ball of radius r"""
    return np.clip(v, -r, r)

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
v = np.array([3.0, -0.4, 1.2, -2.5, 0.05])
print("prox_l1(v, 1)   =", prox_l1(v, 1.0))
# Moreau decomposition: v = prox_{gamma f}(v) + gamma * prox_{f*/gamma}(v/gamma),
# with f = ||.||_1, f* = indicator of the unit l-infinity ball
print("Moreau residual =", np.abs(v - prox_l1(v, 1.0) - proj_linf(v, 1.0)).max())

# firm nonexpansiveness: ||p - q||^2 <= <p - q, u - w>
worst = np.inf
for _ in range(10000):
    u, w = rng.standard_normal(5) * 3, rng.standard_normal(5) * 3
    p, q = prox_l1(u, 0.7), prox_l1(w, 0.7)
    worst = min(worst, (p - q) @ (u - w) - (p - q) @ (p - q))
print(f"min of <p-q,u-w> - ||p-q||^2 over 10^4 pairs: {worst:.2e}")
```

The output is $(2, 0, 0.2, -1.5, 0)$, a Moreau residual of exactly 0, and a minimum of $-7 \times 10^{-15}$ for the firm-nonexpansiveness gap, which is zero up to rounding.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 2

-   $\mathrm{prox}_{\gamma f}(v)$ is the unique minimizer of $f + \frac{1}{2\gamma}\|\cdot - v\|^2$, characterized by $v - p \in \gamma\, \partial f(p)$: an implicit gradient step.
-   Projections, soft thresholding, group shrinkage and linear solves are proximity operators; separable functions have separable, parallel proxes.
-   Minimizers are the fixed points of the prox, and the prox is firmly nonexpansive: these two facts drive every convergence proof of the course.
-   Moreau's decomposition links the prox of $f$ and of $f^*$; the Moreau envelope smooths $f$ with a $\frac1\gamma$-Lipschitz gradient.
:::

## 3. Proximal gradient algorithms: forward–backward and FISTA {#ch3}

Many problems split into a smooth data term and a non-smooth but proximable regularizer. This chapter combines a gradient step on the first with a proximal step on the second, and proves the rates of the plain and accelerated versions.

Throughout the chapter, $F = f + g$ with $f$ convex and $L$-smooth, $g \in \Gamma_0(\mathbb{R}^N)$, and a minimizer $x^\star$ exists.

### Forward–backward splitting

::: thm
[Algorithm 3.1 — Forward–backward (proximal gradient)]{.tag} Choose $x_0$ and steps $\gamma_k \in (0, 2/L)$. Iterate
$$
x_{k+1} = \mathrm{prox}_{\gamma_k g}\big(x_k - \gamma_k \nabla f(x_k)\big) .
$$
The step on $f$ is explicit (forward), the step on $g$ implicit (backward).
:::

Special cases: $g = 0$ gives gradient descent; $f = 0$ gives the proximal point algorithm; $g = \iota_C$ gives projected gradient; $g = \lambda \|\cdot\|_1$ gives **ISTA**, the iterative shrinkage-thresholding algorithm (Daubechies, Defrise and De Mol, 2004).

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.2 — Fixed points]{.tag} For every $\gamma > 0$, $x^\star$ minimizes $F$ if and only if
$$
x^\star = \mathrm{prox}_{\gamma g}\big(x^\star - \gamma \nabla f(x^\star)\big) .
$$

::: proof
By Proposition 2.2, the fixed-point equation reads $-\nabla f(x^\star) \in \partial g(x^\star)$ after division by $\gamma$. By the sum rule, this is
$$
0 \in \nabla f(x^\star) + \partial g(x^\star) = \partial F(x^\star),
$$
and Fermat's rule concludes. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The norm of $x_k - x_{k+1}$, divided by $\gamma_k$, therefore measures optimality and gives a stopping criterion.

:::: prop
[Lemma 3.3 — Key inequality]{.tag} Let $x^+ = \mathrm{prox}_{g/L}\big(x - \nabla f(x)/L\big)$. For every $z$:
$$
F(x^+) \leq F(z) + \frac{L}{2}\big( \|x - z\|^2 - \|x^+ - z\|^2 \big) .
$$

::: proof
Three inequalities, then one identity.

1.  Descent lemma:
    $$
    f(x^+) \leq f(x) + \langle \nabla f(x), x^+ - x \rangle + \tfrac{L}{2}\|x^+ - x\|^2 .
    $$
2.  Convexity of $f$: $f(x) + \langle \nabla f(x), z - x \rangle \leq f(z)$.
3.  By Proposition 2.2, $L(x - x^+) - \nabla f(x) \in \partial g(x^+)$, so
    $$
    g(x^+) \leq g(z) - \langle L(x - x^+) - \nabla f(x),\, z - x^+ \rangle .
    $$
4.  Adding the three, the gradient terms combine into $\langle \nabla f(x), z - x\rangle$ and cancel against item 2:
    $$
    F(x^+) \leq F(z) + \frac{L}{2}\|x^+ - x\|^2 - L \langle x - x^+, z - x^+ \rangle .
    $$
5.  With $a = x - x^+$ and $c = z - x^+$, the identity $\|a\|^2 - 2\langle a, c\rangle = \|a - c\|^2 - \|c\|^2$ turns the last two terms into the claim. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.4 — Rate of forward–backward]{.tag} With $\gamma_k = 1/L$, the values $F(x_k)$ are non-increasing and
$$
F(x_k) - F(x^\star) \leq \frac{L\, \|x_0 - x^\star\|^2}{2k} .
$$
For any constant step in $(0, 2/L)$, the iterates converge to a minimizer (Combettes and Wajs, 2005).

::: proof
Lemma 3.3 with $z = x_k$ gives $F(x_{k+1}) \leq F(x_k) - \frac{L}{2}\|x_{k+1} - x_k\|^2$: monotonicity.

With $z = x^\star$, summing the inequality over the first $k$ steps telescopes, exactly as in Theorem 0.7. The sum of the gaps is at most $\frac{L}{2}\|x_0 - x^\star\|^2$, and the last gap is the smallest. Convergence of the iterates is the averaged-operator argument of [ch. 4](#ch4). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### Acceleration: FISTA

::: thm
[Algorithm 3.5 — FISTA (Beck and Teboulle, 2009)]{.tag} Set $y_1 = x_0$ and $t_1 = 1$. For $k \geq 1$:
$$
x_k = \mathrm{prox}_{g/L}\big(y_k - \tfrac{1}{L}\nabla f(y_k)\big), \qquad t_{k+1} = \frac{1 + \sqrt{1 + 4t_k^2}}{2},
$$
$$
y_{k+1} = x_k + \frac{t_k - 1}{t_{k+1}}\,(x_k - x_{k-1}) .
$$
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.6 — Rate of FISTA]{.tag} The iterates of Algorithm 3.5 satisfy
$$
F(x_k) - F(x^\star) \leq \frac{2L\, \|x_0 - x^\star\|^2}{(k+1)^2} .
$$

::: proof
Two facts on the sequence $t_k$: $t_{k+1}^2 - t_{k+1} = t_k^2$ by construction, and $t_k \geq (k+1)/2$ by induction, since $t_{k+1} \geq t_k + \frac12$.

Write $t = t_{k+1}$ and define $u_k = x_{k-1} + t_k (x_k - x_{k-1})$.

1.  Apply Lemma 3.3 at the point $y_{k+1}$ with $z = (1 - \frac1t) x_k + \frac1t x^\star$.
2.  By convexity, $F(z) \leq (1 - \frac1t) F(x_k) + \frac1t F(x^\star)$.
3.  The definitions give $t\,(y_{k+1} - z) = u_k - x^\star$ and $t\,(x_{k+1} - z) = u_{k+1} - x^\star$.
4.  Multiplying by $t^2$ and using $t^2 - t = t_k^2$, the energy below is non-increasing:
    $$
    E_k = t_k^2 \big(F(x_k) - F(x^\star)\big) + \frac{L}{2}\|u_k - x^\star\|^2 .
    $$
5.  Lemma 3.3 at $x_0$ with $z = x^\star$ gives $E_1 \leq \frac{L}{2}\|x_0 - x^\star\|^2$, since $u_1 = x_1$.

Hence the following bound holds, and $t_k \geq (k+1)/2$ concludes:
$$
t_k^2 \big(F(x_k) - F(x^\star)\big) \leq \frac{L}{2}\|x_0 - x^\star\|^2 .
$$
[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

FISTA is not monotone, and the convergence of its iterates is subtle; Chambolle and Dossal (2015) prove it for the slightly modified sequence $t_k = (k + a - 1)/a$ with $a > 2$.

### Variable metric and line search

::: def
[Definition 3.7 — Variable metric forward–backward]{.tag} For symmetric positive definite matrices $P_k$, the step
$$
x_{k+1} = \mathrm{prox}^{P_k}_{g}\big(x_k - P_k^{-1}\nabla f(x_k)\big), \qquad \mathrm{prox}^{P}_{g}(v) = \operatorname*{argmin}_x \; g(x) + \tfrac12 \|x - v\|_P^2,
$$
replaces $L\, I$ by a majorant metric $P_k$, as in Definition 1.8.

Chouzenoux, Pesquet and Repetti (2014) prove its convergence when $P_k$ satisfies the majorization condition of Definition 1.8, including for non-convex $f$ (ch. 9). The metric prox is explicit when $P_k$ is diagonal and $g$ separable.
:::

When $L$ is unknown, **backtracking** multiplies a trial $L$ by a factor $\eta > 1$ until the descent inequality of Lemma 0.6 holds between $y_k$ and the new point. The rates are kept, with $L$ replaced by $\eta L$ in the worst case (Beck and Teboulle, 2009).

::: ex
[Example 3.8 — ISTA and FISTA on a lasso]{.tag} The code generates a 10-sparse signal in dimension 500 observed through 200 random measurements, and solves the lasso with $\lambda = 0.02$. scikit-learn provides the reference value; it scales the data term by $1/n$, hence $\alpha = \lambda / n$.
:::

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import Lasso

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n, d, s = 200, 500, 10
A = rng.standard_normal((n, d)) / np.sqrt(n)
x_true = np.zeros(d)
x_true[rng.choice(d, s, replace=False)] = rng.choice([-1.0, 1.0], s) * rng.uniform(1, 2, s)
b = A @ x_true + 0.01 * rng.standard_normal(n)
lam = 0.02

F = lambda x: 0.5 * np.sum((A @ x - b) ** 2) + lam * np.abs(x).sum()
soft = lambda v, g: np.sign(v) * np.maximum(np.abs(v) - g, 0.0)
L = np.linalg.norm(A, 2) ** 2

# reference solution: scikit-learn minimises (1/2n)||b - Ax||^2 + alpha ||x||_1
ref = Lasso(alpha=lam / n, fit_intercept=False, tol=1e-12, max_iter=100000).fit(A, b).coef_
F_star = F(ref)

x = np.zeros(d)                          # ISTA = forward-backward
z, y, t = np.zeros(d), np.zeros(d), 1.0  # FISTA
for k in range(1, 301):
    x = soft(x - A.T @ (A @ x - b) / L, lam / L)
    z_new = soft(y - A.T @ (A @ y - b) / L, lam / L)
    t_new = (1 + np.sqrt(1 + 4 * t * t)) / 2
    y = z_new + (t - 1) / t_new * (z_new - z)
    z, t = z_new, t_new
    if k in (10, 50, 300):
        print(f"k={k:5d}  ISTA {F(x) - F_star:.2e}   FISTA {F(z) - F_star:.2e}")

supp = lambda v: set(np.flatnonzero(np.abs(v) > 1e-6))
print("true support recovered by FISTA:", supp(x_true) <= supp(z), "| nonzeros:", len(supp(z)))
print(f"relative error ||x - x_true|| / ||x_true|| = {np.linalg.norm(z - x_true) / np.linalg.norm(x_true):.3f}")
```

The objective gaps are:

| Iteration | ISTA | FISTA |
|---|---|---|
| 10 | 0.52 | 0.42 |
| 50 | 0.29 | $5.8 \times 10^{-4}$ |
| 300 | $2.9 \times 10^{-7}$ | $6.3 \times 10^{-13}$ |

The final estimate has 38 non-zeros: the 10 true ones and 28 spurious ones, all below 0.02 in absolute value. Its relative error is 0.024. Both methods end up converging linearly, because the lasso is strongly convex on the support of the solution; FISTA reaches that regime much earlier.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 3

-   Forward–backward alternates a gradient step on the smooth term and a prox step on the other; minimizers are its fixed points for every step size.
-   One inequality (Lemma 3.3) gives monotonicity and the $O(1/k)$ rate, and, with an energy argument, the $O(1/k^2)$ rate of FISTA.
-   Variable metrics and backtracking adapt the step to the local curvature without knowing $L$.
-   On the lasso, ISTA is soft thresholding after a gradient step; FISTA reaches $10^{-3}$ accuracy in 50 iterations where ISTA is still at 0.29.
:::

## 4. Splitting algorithms: Douglas–Rachford, ADMM and primal–dual methods {#ch4}

Forward–backward needs one smooth term. Total variation $\lambda\|Dx\|_1$, a sum of two constraints, or a non-smooth data term break this assumption. This chapter builds algorithms that only use the proxes of the individual terms and products by linear operators, from one fixed-point theorem.

### Averaged operators

::: def
[Definition 4.1 — Nonexpansive and averaged operators]{.tag} An operator $T : \mathbb{R}^N \to \mathbb{R}^N$ is **nonexpansive** if $\|Tx - Ty\| \leq \|x - y\|$ for all $x, y$.

It is **$\alpha$-averaged**, for $\alpha \in (0, 1)$, if $T = (1 - \alpha) I + \alpha R$ with $R$ nonexpansive. Firmly nonexpansive operators (Proposition 2.5) are exactly the $\frac12$-averaged ones.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.2 — The building blocks are averaged]{.tag}

1.  The **reflected prox** $R_{\gamma f} = 2\,\mathrm{prox}_{\gamma f} - I$ is nonexpansive.
2.  If $f$ is convex and $L$-smooth and $\gamma \in (0, 2/L)$, then $I - \gamma \nabla f$ is $\frac{\gamma L}{2}$-averaged.
3.  A composition of averaged operators is averaged.

::: proof
Item 1: for any $T$, expanding the square gives
$$
\|(2T - I)x - (2T - I)y\|^2 = \|x - y\|^2 - 4\big( \langle Tx - Ty, x - y \rangle - \|Tx - Ty\|^2 \big),
$$
which is at most $\|x - y\|^2$ when $T$ is firmly nonexpansive. Item 2 rests on the Baillon–Haddad theorem, by which $\frac1L \nabla f$ is firmly nonexpansive. Item 3 is a computation on the averaging constants (Bauschke and Combettes, 2011, ch. 4). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.3 — Krasnosel'skii–Mann]{.tag} Let $T$ be $\alpha$-averaged with at least one fixed point, and $x_{k+1} = T x_k$. Then $(x_k)$ converges to a fixed point of $T$, and the fixed-point residual decreases at the rate
$$
\|x_k - T x_k\| \leq \sqrt{\frac{\alpha}{(1 - \alpha)\,(k + 1)}}\; \|x_0 - z\| \qquad \text{for every fixed point } z .
$$

::: proof
Write $T = (1 - \alpha)I + \alpha R$, and let $z = Tz = Rz$.

1.  Take $a = x - z$ and $c = Rx - z$, so that $\|c\| \leq \|a\|$. The identity
    $$
    \|(1 - \alpha)a + \alpha c\|^2 = (1 - \alpha)\|a\|^2 + \alpha\|c\|^2 - \alpha(1 - \alpha)\|a - c\|^2
    $$
    and $x - Tx = \alpha (x - Rx)$ give
    $$
    \|Tx - z\|^2 \leq \|x - z\|^2 - \frac{1 - \alpha}{\alpha}\, \|x - Tx\|^2 .
    $$
2.  The distances to every fixed point decrease (**Fejér monotonicity**), and summing gives
    $$
    \sum_k \|x_k - Tx_k\|^2 \leq \frac{\alpha}{1 - \alpha}\|x_0 - z\|^2 .
    $$
3.  The residuals are non-increasing, because $T$ is nonexpansive and $x_{k+1} = T x_k$:
    $$
    \|x_{k+1} - Tx_{k+1}\| = \|Tx_k - Tx_{k+1}\| \leq \|x_k - x_{k+1}\| .
    $$
    The last of $k + 1$ terms is at most their mean: this is the rate.
4.  The sequence is bounded; by continuity of $T$, its cluster points are fixed points. Fejér monotonicity with respect to such a cluster point forces the whole sequence to converge to it. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

By Proposition 4.2, the forward–backward operator $\mathrm{prox}_{\gamma g} \circ (I - \gamma \nabla f)$ is averaged for $\gamma \in (0, 2/L)$, and its fixed points are the minimizers (Proposition 3.2). Theorem 4.3 thus proves the convergence of the iterates claimed in Theorem 3.4.

### Douglas–Rachford splitting

::: thm
[Algorithm 4.4 — Douglas–Rachford]{.tag} To minimize $f + g$ with $f, g \in \Gamma_0(\mathbb{R}^N)$, choose $\gamma > 0$, $\lambda \in (0, 2)$ and $y_0$. Iterate
$$
x_k = \mathrm{prox}_{\gamma g}(y_k), \qquad w_k = \mathrm{prox}_{\gamma f}(2 x_k - y_k), \qquad y_{k+1} = y_k + \lambda\, (w_k - x_k) .
$$
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.5 — Convergence of Douglas–Rachford]{.tag} If $f + g$ has a minimizer and the relative interiors of $\mathrm{dom} f$ and $\mathrm{dom}\, g$ intersect, then $y_k \to y^\star$, and $x_k$ converges to
$$
x^\star = \mathrm{prox}_{\gamma g}(y^\star) \in \operatorname{argmin}\, (f + g) .
$$

::: proof
*Sketch* for $\lambda = 1$ (Lions and Mercier, 1979; Eckstein and Bertsekas, 1992).

1.  A direct computation shows $y_{k+1} = T y_k$ with $T = \frac12 (I + R_{\gamma f} R_{\gamma g})$.
2.  $R_{\gamma f} R_{\gamma g}$ is nonexpansive (Proposition 4.2), so $T$ is $\frac12$-averaged, and Theorem 4.3 applies.
3.  At a fixed point, $w = x$. Then $y - x \in \gamma\,\partial g(x)$ and $x - y \in \gamma\,\partial f(x)$, whose sum is $0 \in \partial f(x) + \partial g(x)$.

The convergence of $x_k$ itself follows from the continuity of the prox. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Douglas–Rachford uses no gradient and no Lipschitz constant: any $\gamma > 0$ works, although $\gamma$ strongly affects the speed (Example 7.7).

### ADMM

The alternating direction method of multipliers handles a linear coupling between two blocks of variables:
$$
\min_{x, z} \; f(x) + g(z) \quad \text{subject to} \quad A x + B z = c .
$$

::: thm
[Algorithm 4.6 — ADMM, scaled form]{.tag} With a penalty $\rho > 0$ and a scaled multiplier $u$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
x_{k+1} &= \operatorname*{argmin}_x \; f(x) + \tfrac{\rho}{2}\|A x + B z_k - c + u_k\|^2, \\
z_{k+1} &= \operatorname*{argmin}_z \; g(z) + \tfrac{\rho}{2}\|A x_{k+1} + B z - c + u_k\|^2, \\
u_{k+1} &= u_k + A x_{k+1} + B z_{k+1} - c .
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.7 — Convergence of ADMM]{.tag} Assume $f, g \in \Gamma_0$ and that the Lagrangian has a saddle point. Then the residual $A x_k + B z_k - c$ tends to 0, the objective tends to the optimal value, and $\rho u_k$ converges to a dual solution (Boyd et al., 2011, §3.2).

::: proof
*Idea.* ADMM is Douglas–Rachford applied to the Fenchel dual of the problem, with $\gamma = \rho$ (Eckstein and Bertsekas, 1992). Theorem 4.5 on the dual gives the convergence of the multipliers, and the primal statements follow from the optimality conditions of the two subproblems. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 4.8 — ADMM for the lasso and for total variation]{.tag}

-   **Lasso**: $f(x) = \frac12\|Ax - b\|^2$, $g = \lambda\|\cdot\|_1$ and the constraint $x - z = 0$. The second step is soft thresholding at $\lambda / \rho$ of $x_{k+1} + u_k$, and the first solves a linear system:
    $$
    (A^\top A + \rho I)\,x_{k+1} = A^\top b + \rho (z_k - u_k) .
    $$
-   **Total variation denoising**: $f(x) = \frac12 \|x - y\|^2$, $g = \lambda \|\cdot\|_1$, constraint $D x - z = 0$. The $x$-step solves a system with the matrix $I + \rho D^\top D$, tridiagonal in one dimension.

In both cases the matrix does not change with $k$: it is factorized once, and each iteration costs two triangular solves.
:::

Boyd et al. (2011) recommend stopping when both the primal residual $\|A x_k + B z_k - c\|$ and the dual residual $\rho \|A^\top B (z_{k} - z_{k-1})\|$ are small.

### Primal–dual methods

The problem $\min_x g(x) + h(Kx)$ is equivalent to the saddle-point problem
$$
\min_x \max_u \; g(x) + \langle K x, u \rangle - h^*(u),
$$
by Definition 0.8 applied to $h = h^{**}$. Primal–dual methods alternate a prox step in $x$ and one in $u$, and never invert $K$.

::: thm
[Algorithm 4.9 — Chambolle–Pock]{.tag} Choose $\tau, \sigma > 0$ with $\tau \sigma \|K\|^2 < 1$, and set $\bar x_0 = x_0$. Iterate
$$
u_{k+1} = \mathrm{prox}_{\sigma h^*}(u_k + \sigma K \bar x_k), \qquad x_{k+1} = \mathrm{prox}_{\tau g}(x_k - \tau K^\top u_{k+1}), \qquad \bar x_{k+1} = 2 x_{k+1} - x_k .
$$
The prox of $h^*$ comes from that of $h$ by the Moreau decomposition (Theorem 2.6).
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.10 — Convergence of Chambolle–Pock]{.tag} If a saddle point exists and $\tau\sigma\|K\|^2 < 1$, then $(x_k, u_k)$ converges to a saddle point, and the primal–dual gap of the averaged iterates decreases as $O(1/k)$ (Chambolle and Pock, 2011).

::: proof
*Idea.* The iteration is a proximal point algorithm in the product space for the metric
$$
M = \begin{pmatrix} \tau^{-1} I & -K^\top \\ -K & \sigma^{-1} I \end{pmatrix},
$$
whose Schur complement $\tau^{-1} I - \sigma K^\top K$ is positive definite exactly when $\tau\sigma\|K\|^2 < 1$ (He and Yuan, 2012). Proposition 2.4 and Theorem 4.3 then apply in the norm of $M$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Condat (2013) and Vũ (2013) add a smooth term $f$ with an $L$-Lipschitz gradient to the primal step:
$$
x_{k+1} = \mathrm{prox}_{\tau g}\big(x_k - \tau (\nabla f(x_k) + K^\top u_{k+1})\big), \qquad \text{with} \quad \frac{1}{\tau} - \sigma \|K\|^2 > \frac{L}{2} .
$$
The result handles $f + g + h \circ K$ with only explicit operations: the most flexible of the splitting algorithms.

::: ex
[Example 4.11 — Total variation denoising in one dimension]{.tag} A piecewise-constant signal of length 500 with noise of standard deviation 0.5 is denoised by minimizing $\frac12\|x - y\|^2 + \lambda \|Dx\|_1$ with $\lambda = 1$.

For Chambolle–Pock, $g = \frac12\|\cdot - y\|^2$, $h = \lambda\|\cdot\|_1$ and $K = D$. Then $h^*$ is the indicator of $[-\lambda, \lambda]^{N-1}$, whose prox is a clipping.

Since $\|D\|^2 < 4$, the choice $\tau = \sigma = 0.49$ is admissible.
:::

```python
import numpy as np
import scipy.sparse as sp
from scipy.sparse.linalg import splu

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
N, lam = 500, 1.0
x_clean = np.repeat([0.0, 2.0, -1.0, 1.0, 0.0], N // 5)       # piecewise constant
y = x_clean + 0.5 * rng.standard_normal(N)
D = sp.diags([-np.ones(N - 1), np.ones(N - 1)], [0, 1], shape=(N - 1, N)).tocsr()
F = lambda x: 0.5 * np.sum((x - y) ** 2) + lam * np.abs(D @ x).sum()

def chambolle_pock(iters, tau=0.49, sigma=0.49):        # tau * sigma * ||D||^2 < 1
    x, xbar, u = y.copy(), y.copy(), np.zeros(N - 1)
    for _ in range(iters):
        u = np.clip(u + sigma * (D @ xbar), -lam, lam)    # prox of sigma h*, h = lam ||.||_1
        x_new = (x - tau * (D.T @ u) + tau * y) / (1 + tau)  # prox of tau g, g = 0.5||. - y||^2
        xbar, x = 2 * x_new - x, x_new
    return x

def admm(iters, rho=1.0):
    solve = splu((sp.eye(N) + rho * D.T @ D).tocsc()).solve   # factorised once
    z, w = np.zeros(N - 1), np.zeros(N - 1)
    for _ in range(iters):
        x = solve(y + rho * (D.T @ (z - w)))
        Dx = D @ x
        z = np.sign(Dx + w) * np.maximum(np.abs(Dx + w) - lam / rho, 0.0)
        w = w + Dx - z
    return x

F_star = F(chambolle_pock(20000))
for k in (50, 200, 1000):
    print(f"k={k:5d}  Chambolle-Pock {F(chambolle_pock(k)) - F_star:.2e}   ADMM {F(admm(k)) - F_star:.2e}")
x = chambolle_pock(20000)
print(f"RMSE noisy {np.sqrt(np.mean((y - x_clean)**2)):.3f} -> denoised {np.sqrt(np.mean((x - x_clean)**2)):.3f}")
```

| Iterations | Chambolle–Pock gap | ADMM gap |
|---|---|---|
| 50 | 1.16 | 0.31 |
| 200 | $8.1 \times 10^{-2}$ | $1.7 \times 10^{-2}$ |
| 1000 | $1.0 \times 10^{-3}$ | $1.0 \times 10^{-5}$ |

The root-mean-square error drops from 0.507 to 0.123. ADMM converges faster per iteration but solves a linear system at each step. Chambolle–Pock only multiplies by $D$ and $D^\top$: on a large two-dimensional image with general boundary conditions, it is the method whose iterations stay cheap and parallel.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 4

-   Proxes are firmly nonexpansive, reflected proxes nonexpansive, and compositions of averaged operators averaged; the Krasnosel'skii–Mann theorem makes every such iteration converge, with residual $O(1/\sqrt{k})$.
-   Douglas–Rachford minimizes $f + g$ with the two proxes only and any $\gamma > 0$; ADMM is Douglas–Rachford on the dual.
-   Chambolle–Pock handles $g + h \circ K$ with products by $K$ and $K^\top$ under $\tau\sigma\|K\|^2 < 1$; Condat–Vũ adds a smooth term.
-   The choice between them is a choice of which operations are cheap at scale: linear solves (ADMM) or matrix–vector products (primal–dual).
:::

## 5. Majorization–Minimization methods {#ch5}

Instead of minimizing a hard function directly, Majorization–Minimization (MM) minimizes, at each step, a simpler function that lies above it and touches it at the current point. Gradient descent, half-quadratic algorithms, iteratively reweighted least squares and EM are all instances.

### The MM principle

::: def
[Definition 5.1 — Tangent majorant and MM iteration]{.tag} A function $h(\cdot \mid y)$ is a **tangent majorant** of $F$ at $y$ if
$$
F(x) \leq h(x \mid y) \ \text{ for all } x, \qquad F(y) = h(y \mid y) .
$$
The MM algorithm computes $x_{k+1} \in \operatorname{argmin}_x h(x \mid x_k)$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.2 — MM decreases the objective]{.tag} The MM iterates satisfy $F(x_{k+1}) \leq F(x_k)$.

::: proof
The chain
$$
F(x_{k+1}) \leq h(x_{k+1} \mid x_k) \leq h(x_k \mid x_k) = F(x_k)
$$
uses majorization, then the definition of $x_{k+1}$ as a minimizer, then tangency. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Monotonicity holds without convexity, which makes MM popular for non-convex models. The art is to choose a majorant that is tight enough to make progress and simple enough to minimize.

### Building majorants

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.3 — Four constructions]{.tag}

1.  **Lipschitz gradient.** If $F$ is $L$-smooth, the descent lemma gives a quadratic majorant with curvature $L\,I$; its minimizer is the gradient step with step $1/L$.
2.  **Curvature matrix.** If there are symmetric positive definite $A(y)$ with
    $$
    F(x) \leq F(y) + \langle \nabla F(y), x - y \rangle + \tfrac12 \|x - y\|^2_{A(y)},
    $$
    the MM step is the preconditioned step $x^+ = y - A(y)^{-1}\nabla F(y)$ of Definition 1.8.
3.  **Half-quadratic.** Let $\varphi : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be even and differentiable, with $u \mapsto \varphi(\sqrt{u})$ concave on $[0, \infty)$, and let $\omega(s) = \varphi'(s)/s$. Then for all $t$ and $s \neq 0$:
    $$
    \varphi(t) \leq \varphi(s) + \frac{\omega(s)}{2}\,(t^2 - s^2) .
    $$
4.  **Absolute value.** For $s \neq 0$, $|t| \leq \frac{t^2}{2|s|} + \frac{|s|}{2}$, by the inequality between arithmetic and geometric means.

::: proof
Item 3: $\psi(u) = \varphi(\sqrt u)$ is concave, so it lies below its tangent at $v = s^2$:
$$
\psi(u) \leq \psi(v) + \psi'(v)\,(u - v) .
$$
With $u = t^2$ and $\psi'(v) = \varphi'(s)/(2s) = \omega(s)/2$, this is the claim. Items 1, 2 and 4 are direct. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The hyperbolic potential $\varphi(t) = \sqrt{t^2 + \delta^2}$, a smooth version of $|t|$ that preserves edges, satisfies item 3 with $\omega(s) = 1/\sqrt{s^2 + \delta^2}$. So does the Cauchy potential $\log(1 + t^2/\delta^2)$, which is not convex.

Item 3 is the majorant behind the multiplicative half-quadratic form of Geman and Reynolds (1992). The additive form of Geman and Yang (1995) corresponds instead to a majorant of constant curvature, as in item 1.

For a penalty $\sum_i \varphi([Dx]_i)$, item 3 replaces each term by a weighted square, and the MM step solves a weighted least-squares problem: this is **iteratively reweighted least squares** (IRLS).

::: ex
[Example 5.4 — EM is an MM algorithm]{.tag} Let a model $p(y, z; \theta)$ have a latent variable $z$, and let $q_k(z) = p(z \mid y; \theta_k)$ be the posterior at the current parameter. By Jensen's inequality for the concave logarithm:
$$
-\log p(y; \theta) = -\log \sum_z q_k(z)\, \frac{p(y, z; \theta)}{q_k(z)} \leq -\sum_z q_k(z) \log \frac{p(y, z; \theta)}{q_k(z)} .
$$
Equality holds at $\theta = \theta_k$, so the right-hand side is a tangent majorant of the negative log-likelihood. Minimizing it is the M-step of EM, and computing $q_k$ is the E-step. Proposition 5.2 recovers the monotonicity of EM, studied in [Computational Statistics](../s1-computational-statistics/index.html).
:::

### Convergence of quadratic MM

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.5 — Convergence of MM with quadratic majorants]{.tag} Let $F$ be continuously differentiable and bounded below, with majorants as in Proposition 5.3, item 2, and $\nu I \preceq A(y) \preceq \nu' I$ for all $y$, with $0 < \nu \leq \nu'$. Then:

1.  $F(x_k)$ decreases, the gradients are square-summable and $\nabla F(x_k) \to 0$:
    $$
    \sum_k \|\nabla F(x_k)\|^2 \leq 2\nu' \big(F(x_0) - \inf F\big) ;
    $$
2.  $\|x_{k+1} - x_k\| \leq \|\nabla F(x_k)\| / \nu \to 0$;
3.  if $F$ is convex and coercive, every cluster point of $(x_k)$ minimizes $F$, and $F(x_k) \to \min F$.

::: proof
Write $g_k = \nabla F(x_k)$ and $A_k = A(x_k)$.

1.  The minimizer of the majorant is $x_{k+1} = x_k - A_k^{-1} g_k$, and the minimum value is $F(x_k) - \frac12 g_k^\top A_k^{-1} g_k$.
2.  Since $A_k^{-1} \succeq I / \nu'$, majorization gives $F(x_{k+1}) \leq F(x_k) - \|g_k\|^2 / (2\nu')$.
3.  Summing over $k$ bounds $\sum_k \|g_k\|^2$ by $2\nu'(F(x_0) - \inf F)$. Item 2 follows from $\|A_k^{-1}\| \leq 1/\nu$.
4.  If $F$ is convex and coercive, the iterates stay in a bounded sublevel set. At a cluster point the gradient vanishes by continuity, so it is a minimizer, and the decreasing values converge to $\min F$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

If moreover $\nabla F$ is Lipschitz and $F$ has the Kurdyka–Łojasiewicz property, which semi-algebraic functions satisfy, every bounded MM sequence converges as a whole, even without convexity (Attouch, Bolte and Svaiter, 2013); see [ch. 9](#ch9).

### MM at scale: the memory-gradient subspace method

For a large image, the half-quadratic step solves a linear system with the matrix $A(x_k)$ at every iteration, which is expensive. The subspace method minimizes the same majorant only over a small subspace.

:::: thm
[Algorithm 5.6 — 3MG, the MM memory-gradient algorithm]{.tag} At iteration $k$, form the $N \times 2$ matrix of directions $S_k = [\,-\nabla F(x_k),\; x_k - x_{k-1}\,]$, then
$$
u_k = -\big(S_k^\top A(x_k)\, S_k\big)^{\dagger} S_k^\top \nabla F(x_k), \qquad x_{k+1} = x_k + S_k u_k .
$$
The step costs two products by $A(x_k)$ and the solution of a $2 \times 2$ system: no large linear system is ever solved.

::: proof
*Why Theorem 5.5 still applies.* The subspace contains $-g_k$, so the minimum of the majorant over it is at most its minimum along $-g_k$:
$$
F(x_k) - \frac{\|g_k\|^4}{2\, g_k^\top A_k g_k} \leq F(x_k) - \frac{\|g_k\|^2}{2\nu'} .
$$
This is the decrease used in step 2 of the proof of Theorem 5.5. Chouzenoux, Idier and Moussaoui (2011) prove the convergence of 3MG under these assumptions and study its speed on image restoration. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The second direction acts as a memory, like the momentum of Algorithm 1.5, but its weight is optimized at each step rather than prescribed.

A **separable** majorant, with $A(y)$ diagonal, is the other road to scale: Proposition 1.9 builds one from any symmetric matrix. Then every coordinate is updated independently, in parallel, which is how classical multiplicative algorithms such as the non-negative matrix factorization updates of Lee and Seung (2001) work.

::: ex
[Example 5.7 — Edge-preserving denoising]{.tag} A piecewise-constant signal of length 2000 with noise of standard deviation 0.5 is denoised by minimizing
$$
F(x) = \tfrac12\|x - y\|^2 + \lambda \sum_i \sqrt{[Dx]_i^2 + \delta^2}, \qquad \lambda = 1, \ \delta = 0.05 .
$$
The half-quadratic majorant has $A(x) = I + \lambda D^\top W(x) D$, with $W(x)$ the diagonal of the weights $\omega([Dx]_i)$. The code compares the exact MM step (a sparse solve), 3MG and gradient descent with the global constant $L = 1 + 4\lambda/\delta = 81$.
:::

```python
import numpy as np
import scipy.sparse as sp
from scipy.sparse.linalg import spsolve

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
N, lam, delta = 2000, 1.0, 0.05
x_clean = np.repeat([0.0, 2.0, -1.0, 1.0, 0.0], N // 5)
y = x_clean + 0.5 * rng.standard_normal(N)
D = sp.diags([-np.ones(N - 1), np.ones(N - 1)], [0, 1], shape=(N - 1, N)).tocsr()

phi = lambda t: np.sqrt(t ** 2 + delta ** 2)          # hyperbolic (smoothed TV) potential
F = lambda x: 0.5 * np.sum((x - y) ** 2) + lam * phi(D @ x).sum()
grad = lambda x: x - y + lam * (D.T @ ((D @ x) / phi(D @ x)))
weights = lambda x: 1.0 / phi(D @ x)                  # omega(t) = phi'(t) / t

def mm_halfquadratic(iters):                           # exact minimisation of the majorant
    x = y.copy()
    for _ in range(iters):
        A = sp.eye(N) + lam * D.T @ sp.diags(weights(x)) @ D
        x = spsolve(A.tocsc(), y)
    return x

def mm_subspace(iters):                                # 3MG: majorant minimised on span(-g, x - x_prev)
    x, x_prev = y.copy(), y.copy()
    for k in range(iters):
        g, w = grad(x), weights(x)
        S = np.column_stack([-g, x - x_prev]) if k else -g[:, None]
        AS = S + lam * (D.T @ (w[:, None] * (D @ S)))  # A(x) S without forming A(x)
        u = np.linalg.solve(S.T @ AS, -S.T @ g)
        x_prev, x = x, x + S @ u
    return x

def gradient_descent(iters):
    L = 1 + 4 * lam / delta                            # Lipschitz bound: ||D||^2 <= 4, phi'' <= 1/delta
    x = y.copy()
    for _ in range(iters):
        x = x - grad(x) / L
    return x

F_star = F(mm_halfquadratic(300))
gap = lambda x: abs(F(x) - F_star)
for k in (10, 50, 200):
    print(f"k={k:4d}  MM-HQ {gap(mm_halfquadratic(k)):.2e}   "
          f"3MG {gap(mm_subspace(k)):.2e}   GD {gap(gradient_descent(k)):.2e}")
vals = []
x = y.copy()
for _ in range(10):                                    # MM is monotone: F decreases at every step
    A = sp.eye(N) + lam * D.T @ sp.diags(weights(x)) @ D
    x = spsolve(A.tocsc(), y)
    vals.append(F(x))
print("monotone decrease:", bool(np.all(np.diff(vals) <= 1e-12)))
```

| Iterations | MM, exact step | 3MG | Gradient descent |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10 | $1.3 \times 10^{-2}$ | 11.8 | 383 |
| 50 | $2.4 \times 10^{-9}$ | $2.8 \times 10^{-7}$ | 25.6 |
| 200 | below $10^{-12}$ | below $10^{-12}$ | $5.9 \times 10^{-2}$ |

The exact MM step converges in fewer iterations, but each one solves a sparse system. 3MG needs a few more iterations at the cost of a gradient step, and it is the version that scales to large two-dimensional problems. Gradient descent pays for the global constant $L = 81$, set by the sharpest edge, while the majorant adapts its curvature locally.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 5

-   MM minimizes a tangent majorant at each step, and the objective decreases monotonically, with or without convexity.
-   Majorants come from the descent lemma, curvature matrices, concavity of $\varphi(\sqrt{\cdot})$ (half-quadratic, IRLS) and Jensen's inequality (EM).
-   With curvature matrices between $\nu I$ and $\nu' I$, the gradients are square-summable; with convexity and coercivity, MM converges to a minimizer.
-   3MG minimizes the majorant over a two-dimensional memory-gradient subspace: no large system, and, on this example, an objective gap 30 times smaller than gradient descent after 10 iterations and $10^8$ times smaller after 50.
:::

## 6. Stochastic and block-coordinate methods for large data sets {#ch6}

When the objective is an average over $n = 10^9$ samples, or has $10^9$ variables, even one exact gradient is too expensive. This chapter replaces it by a cheap unbiased estimate (stochastic methods) or by a partial derivative (coordinate methods), and measures what is lost and how to recover it.

The objective is a finite sum, as in Example 1.1:
$$
F(x) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x) .
$$
One full gradient costs $n$ sample gradients: a **pass** over the data.

### Stochastic gradient

::: thm
[Algorithm 6.1 — Stochastic gradient (SGD)]{.tag} Draw $i_t$ uniformly in $\{1, \dots, n\}$ and step along the sample gradient:
$$
x_{t+1} = x_t - \gamma_t\, \nabla f_{i_t}(x_t) .
$$
The direction is unbiased: its conditional expectation is $\nabla F(x_t)$.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 6.2 — SGD on a strongly convex function]{.tag} Let $F$ be $\mu$-strongly convex with minimizer $x^\star$ on a closed convex set $X$. Run projected SGD, $x_{t+1} = P_X(x_t - \gamma_t g_t)$.

Assume that $g_t$ is unbiased given $x_t$ and that $\mathbb{E}\|g_t\|^2 \leq G^2$. With $\gamma_t = 1/(\mu t)$, for every $t \geq 2$:
$$
\mathbb{E}\, \|x_t - x^\star\|^2 \leq \frac{2 G^2}{\mu^2\, t} .
$$

::: proof
Write $a_t = \mathbb{E}\|x_t - x^\star\|^2$ and $c = G^2/\mu^2$.

1.  The projection is nonexpansive and fixes $x^\star$, so
    $$
    \|x_{t+1} - x^\star\|^2 \leq \|x_t - x^\star\|^2 - 2\gamma_t \langle g_t, x_t - x^\star \rangle + \gamma_t^2 \|g_t\|^2 .
    $$
2.  Strong convexity and the optimality of $x^\star$ on $X$ give
    $$
    \langle \nabla F(x), x - x^\star \rangle \geq \mu \|x - x^\star\|^2 .
    $$
    Taking expectations: $a_{t+1} \leq (1 - 2/t)\, a_t + c / t^2$.
3.  At $t = 1$ the coefficient of $a_1$ is negative, so $a_2 \leq c$, which is the claim at $t = 2$.
4.  If $a_t \leq 2c/t$ with $t \geq 2$, then $a_{t+1} \leq c\,(2t - 3)/t^2 \leq 2c/(t + 1)$, since $(2t - 3)(t + 1) \leq 2t^2$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The rate $O(1/t)$ is slow compared with the linear rate of gradient descent, but each step costs $1/n$ of a pass. The noise is the limit: with a constant step, SGD only reaches a neighborhood of $x^\star$ whose size is proportional to the step and to the variance of the sample gradients.

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.3 — Mini-batches divide the variance]{.tag} Let $g = \frac1B \sum_{b=1}^B \nabla f_{i_b}(x)$ with $i_1, \dots, i_B$ independent and uniform. Then $\mathbb{E}\, g = \nabla F(x)$ and
$$
\mathbb{E}\, \|g - \nabla F(x)\|^2 = \frac{1}{B}\, \mathbb{E}\, \|\nabla f_{i}(x) - \nabla F(x)\|^2 .
$$

::: proof
The terms $\nabla f_{i_b}(x) - \nabla F(x)$ are independent and centred, so the cross terms of the squared norm of their sum vanish in expectation. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The $B$ sample gradients of a mini-batch are independent computations: on $B$ workers, a mini-batch step takes the time of one sample gradient. This is the root of data parallelism ([ch. 7](#ch7)).

### Variance reduction

The variance of SGD does not vanish at the solution, because the individual gradients $\nabla f_i(x^\star)$ are not zero. Variance-reduced methods correct each sample gradient with a reference point.

::: thm
[Algorithm 6.4 — SVRG (Johnson and Zhang, 2013)]{.tag} At each outer step $s$, keep a snapshot $\tilde x$ and its full gradient $\tilde g = \nabla F(\tilde x)$. Then run $m$ inner steps
$$
x_{t+1} = x_t - \eta\, \big( \nabla f_{i_t}(x_t) - \nabla f_{i_t}(\tilde x) + \tilde g \big),
$$
and take as new snapshot one of the inner iterates.
:::

The direction is still unbiased, and its variance tends to zero as both $x_t$ and $\tilde x$ approach $x^\star$.

:::: thm
[Theorem 6.5 — Linear convergence of SVRG]{.tag} Let each $f_i$ be convex and $L$-smooth and $F$ be $\mu$-strongly convex. Take $\eta < 1/(4L)$, $m$ large enough that
$$
\rho = \frac{1}{\mu \eta\, (1 - 2L\eta)\, m} + \frac{2L\eta}{1 - 2L\eta} < 1,
$$
and the new snapshot uniformly among the inner iterates. Then
$$
\mathbb{E}\,[F(\tilde x_s) - F(x^\star)] \leq \rho^s\, [F(\tilde x_0) - F(x^\star)] .
$$

::: proof
*Key step* (Johnson and Zhang, 2013, Theorem 1). Smoothness and convexity of each $f_i$ bound the second moment of the corrected direction $v_t$ by the suboptimality of the two points:
$$
\mathbb{E}\, \|v_t\|^2 \leq 4L\, \big[ F(x_t) - F(x^\star) + F(\tilde x) - F(x^\star) \big] .
$$
Plugging this into the expansion of step 1 of Theorem 6.2, summing over the inner loop and using strong convexity at $\tilde x$ gives the contraction factor $\rho$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

With $\eta = 0.1/L$ and $m = 50 L/\mu$, the factor is $\rho = \frac{1}{5 \times 0.8} + \frac{0.2}{0.8} = 0.5$.

Each outer step costs $n + 2m$ sample gradients. Reaching accuracy $\varepsilon$ therefore costs $O((n + L/\mu) \log(1/\varepsilon))$ sample gradients, against $O(n\, \kappa \log(1/\varepsilon))$ for gradient descent: the condition number and the number of samples now add instead of multiplying.

SAGA (Defazio, Bach and Lacoste-Julien, 2014) keeps a table of the last gradient of each $f_i$ instead of a snapshot. It needs no full passes and handles a proximal term.

::: ex
[Example 6.6 — Logistic regression with three methods]{.tag} An $\ell_2$-regularized logistic regression with $n = 5000$ samples, $d = 20$ features and $\mu = 10^{-3}$ is solved with a budget of 20 passes over the data.

-   Full gradient descent uses the step $1/L$.
-   SGD uses $1/(L_{\max} + \mu t)$, where $L_{\max}$ bounds the smoothness of every $f_i$.
-   SVRG uses $\eta = 0.5/L_{\max}$, beyond the theoretical $1/(4L_{\max})$, as is common in practice. One outer step with $m = n$ costs three passes (a full gradient, then two sample gradients per inner step), so it gets 6 outer steps.
:::

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import minimize

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n, d, mu = 5000, 20, 1e-3
A = rng.standard_normal((n, d))
b = np.sign(A @ rng.standard_normal(d) + 0.5 * rng.standard_normal(n))

def F(x):
    return np.mean(np.logaddexp(0, -b * (A @ x))) + 0.5 * mu * x @ x
def grad_i(x, i):                                  # gradient of the i-th term f_i
    s = -b[i] / (1 + np.exp(b[i] * (A[i] @ x)))
    return s * A[i] + mu * x
def full_grad(x):
    s = -b / (1 + np.exp(b * (A @ x)))
    return A.T @ s / n + mu * x

F_star = minimize(F, np.zeros(d), jac=full_grad, method="L-BFGS-B", tol=1e-14).fun
L = np.linalg.norm(A, 2) ** 2 / (4 * n) + mu        # smoothness of F
L_max = np.max(np.sum(A ** 2, axis=1)) / 4 + mu     # smoothness of the worst f_i
passes = 20                                          # budget: 20 passes over the data

x = np.zeros(d)                                      # full gradient descent: 1 pass per step
for _ in range(passes):
    x -= full_grad(x) / L
gd = F(x) - F_star

x = np.zeros(d)                                      # SGD, decreasing step 1 / (L_max + mu t)
for t, i in enumerate(rng.integers(n, size=passes * n)):
    x -= grad_i(x, i) / (L_max + mu * t)
sgd = F(x) - F_star

eta = 0.5 / L_max                                    # SVRG: snapshot every n inner steps
x_tilde, used = np.zeros(d), 0
while used + 3 <= passes:                            # each outer loop costs 3n sample gradients
    g_tilde, x = full_grad(x_tilde), x_tilde.copy()
    for i in rng.integers(n, size=n):
        x -= eta * (grad_i(x, i) - grad_i(x_tilde, i) + g_tilde)
    x_tilde, used = x, used + 3
svrg = F(x_tilde) - F_star
print(f"after {passes} passes: GD {gd:.1e}   SGD {sgd:.1e}   SVRG {svrg:.1e}")
print(f"condition number L/mu = {L / mu:.0f},  L_max/L = {L_max / L:.1f}")
```

After 20 passes the objective gaps are
$$
\text{GD: } 2.5 \times 10^{-2}, \qquad \text{SGD: } 2.0 \times 10^{-3}, \qquad \text{SVRG: } 3.0 \times 10^{-8} .
$$
The condition number is 285 and $L_{\max}/L = 41.4$. SGD makes fast early progress and then stalls on its variance; SVRG keeps the cheap steps and converges linearly.

### Randomized block-coordinate descent

When the number of variables is huge, one can update a single block of coordinates at a time. Write $x = (x_1, \dots, x_p)$ in blocks and let $L_i$ be the Lipschitz constant of the block gradient $\nabla_i F$ with respect to changes of block $i$.

::: thm
[Algorithm 6.7 — Randomized block-coordinate descent]{.tag} Draw a block $i_k$ uniformly in $\{1, \dots, p\}$ and update only that block:
$$
x_{i_k} \leftarrow x_{i_k} - \frac{1}{L_{i_k}}\, \nabla_{i_k} F(x) .
$$
For a separable term $g = \sum_i g_i$, the step becomes a block prox:
$$
x_{i} \leftarrow \mathrm{prox}_{g_i / L_i}\big(x_i - \nabla_i F(x)/L_i\big) .
$$
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 6.8 — Linear rate of coordinate descent]{.tag} If $F$ is $\mu$-strongly convex and every $L_i \leq L_{\max}$, then
$$
\mathbb{E}\, [F(x_k)] - F^\star \leq \Big(1 - \frac{\mu}{p\, L_{\max}}\Big)^k \big(F(x_0) - F^\star\big) .
$$

::: proof
1.  The descent lemma along block $i$ gives $F(x^+) \leq F(x) - \|\nabla_i F(x)\|^2 / (2L_{\max})$.
2.  Averaging over the uniform block:
    $$
    \mathbb{E}\, F(x^+) \leq F(x) - \frac{\|\nabla F(x)\|^2}{2 p L_{\max}} .
    $$
3.  Minimizing the strong-convexity lower bound over the second point gives the Polyak–Łojasiewicz inequality:
    $$
    \|\nabla F(x)\|^2 \geq 2\mu\, \big(F(x) - F^\star\big) .
    $$
4.  Combining 2 and 3 gives a contraction by $1 - \mu/(p L_{\max})$ in expectation; iterate. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

One block step costs about $1/p$ of a gradient when partial derivatives are cheap, for instance for $F(x) = f(Ax)$ with the residual kept up to date. Per pass, the contraction is about $e^{-\mu/L_{\max}}$, against $e^{-\mu/L}$ for gradient descent.

Since $L_{\max} \leq L \leq p L_{\max}$, the gain per pass lies between 1 and $p$. There is no gain for a separable $F$, where $L = L_{\max}$. The gain is largest when the coordinates are strongly coupled, for instance for least squares with highly correlated columns, where $L$ approaches $p L_{\max}$.

Nesterov (2012) gives the general analysis with non-uniform sampling; the proximal and parallel versions (Richtárik and Takáč, 2014 and 2016) lead to [ch. 7](#ch7).

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 6

-   SGD replaces the gradient of a finite sum by one sample gradient; with steps $1/(\mu t)$ it reaches $O(1/t)$ in expected squared distance.
-   Mini-batches divide the variance by the batch size and are computed in parallel.
-   SVRG and SAGA remove the variance at the solution and recover a linear rate with total cost $O((n + \kappa)\log(1/\varepsilon))$.
-   Randomized coordinate descent contracts by $1 - \mu/(pL_{\max})$ per block step, and beats gradient descent when the coordinate constants are small compared with $L$.
:::

## 7. Parallel optimization {#ch7}

A multicore machine or a cluster offers $p$ processors. This chapter asks which parts of an optimization algorithm can run simultaneously, how much time that saves, and what must change in the algorithm when updates happen at the same time.

### Architectures and speedup

::: def
[Definition 7.1 — Parallel architectures and synchronization]{.tag}

-   **Shared memory** (multicore): all threads read and write the same iterate in RAM; communication is cheap, but simultaneous writes conflict.
-   **Distributed memory** (cluster, several GPUs): each node holds its own data and variables and communicates by messages, whose cost is modelled as a fixed latency plus a time per number sent.
-   **Synchronous** algorithms wait at a barrier at each iteration for the slowest worker; **asynchronous** ones let each worker proceed with possibly outdated information.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 7.2 — Amdahl's law]{.tag} If a fraction $s$ of the work is sequential and the rest is perfectly parallel, the speedup on $p$ processors is
$$
S(p) = \frac{1}{s + (1 - s)/p} \leq \frac{1}{s} .
$$

::: proof
The time on $p$ processors is $s\,T + (1 - s)\,T/p$, where $T$ is the sequential time. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

With $s = 0.05$ and $p = 32$, the speedup is only $1/(0.05 + 0.95/32) = 12.5$, and no number of processors exceeds 20. The sequential part of an optimization algorithm is typically a reduction (an average, a norm, a step-size computation) or a synchronization.

:::: prop
